# Nearly Optimal Fixed-Confidence Best-Arm Identification with 1-Bit Feedback

**Abstract**

We study fixed-confidence best-arm identification under strict 1-bit feedback constraints. At each round, the learner selects an arm and a query set, and receives only a single bit indicating whether the sampled reward belongs to that set. We consider a distribution-free finite-variance setting with arm-wise localization, where direct empirical mean estimation is no longer available and clipping becomes unavoidable. We first formulate a time-uniform 1-bit mean-estimation primitive based on randomized threshold queries and a clipped tail-integral identity. We then embed this primitive into candidate-challenger best-arm identification algorithms. A fixed- clipping algorithm gives a simple anytime \((\epsilon,\delta)\)-PAC guarantee, while a phased adaptive-clipping algorithm matches the clipping level to the current resolution and yields a gap-adaptive sample complexity. We also prove a _K_-arm worst-case information-theoretic lower bound showing that the logarithmic penalty caused by finite-variance 1-bit feedback is intrinsic. This bound matches the leading dependence of the phased algorithm up to lower-order loglog factors.

### 1 Introduction

Fixed-confidence best-arm identification (BAI) is the problem of identifying an optimal, or near- optimal, arm with high probability while using as few samples as possible [6, 14, 8]. Classical formulations assume that each pull reveals the reward value itself, so that empirical means and confidence intervals can be formed directly. In this paper, we study BAI under strict _1-bit_ feedback constraints: at each round, the learner selects an arm and a query set, and receives only a single bit indicating whether the sampled reward belongs to that set. Two concrete applications instantiate the threshold-query subclass of this model.

Uplink-constrained sensing. A controller selects one of _K_ sensing locations or configurations. A fresh scalar measurement \(X_{k,t}\sim\nu_k\) is compared locally with a programmed threshold _q<sub>t</sub>_, and the device sends only \(Y_t=\mathbf{1}\{X_{k,t}\ge q_t\}\). The controller seeks a location whose mean pollutant concentration or diagnostic score is within \(\varepsilon\) of the largest, with confidence \(1-\delta\), before prioritizing an inspection or deploying an expensive high-resolution monitor. Quantized scalar sensing motivates this response mechanism [23]; adaptive arm selection and fixed-confidence identification are our specialization.

Posted pricing. A seller selects a buyer population _k_, posts a price _q<sub>t</sub>_ to a fresh buyer with hidden valuation \(X_{k,t}\sim\nu_k\), and observes only the purchase bit \(Y_t=\mathbf{1}\{X_{k,t}\ge q_t\}\). This is the accept/reject mechanism of posted-price auctions [17]. Screening _K_ populations for an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal mean valuation gives a threshold-query BAI problem. The objective here is mean valuation; revenue maximization is a different objective.

In both applications, the learner chooses the threshold before the fresh sample is drawn. We constrain the response to one bit and assume the threshold can be supplied through a downlink or a programmable comparator. Thus these mechanisms support the queries used by our algorithms.

We focus on distribution-free fixed-confidence BAI under a finite-variance assumption. The main challenge is that under 1-bit feedback, best-arm identification can no longer rely on direct empirical estimates of arm means. Even estimating the mean of a single arm becomes nontrivial: one must reconstruct a real-valued quantity from binary threshold queries while controlling both stochastic variance and approximation bias. Under only a second-moment assumption, this naturally leads to a clipping or truncation step \[20, 21\], and hence to a nontrivial bias–variance tradeoff. In the bandit setting, this difficulty is compounded by adaptivity: the learner must compare arms and decide when to stop using confidence intervals that remain valid uniformly over time, even though the number of pulls allocated to each arm is itself data-dependent. A fixed-target 1-bit mean estimator is not directly sufficient for a per-pull rule whose local sample counts are random and data-dependent. One needs either a time-uniform confidence sequence, as in Theorem 5, or an outer wrapper that invokes fixed-target estimators at prespecified checkpoints with simultaneous confidence control, as in phased successive elimination.

Our approach is organized around this clipping difficulty. The clipping level controls a bias-variance tradeoff: a larger level reduces clipping bias but enlarges both the variance proxy and the almost-sure range of the 1-bit estimator. The ideal choice therefore depends on the scale at which arms must be distinguished, a scale governed by the unknown gaps. We address this through a 1-bit estimator with time-uniform validity, embedded into two complementary BAI strategies: a fixed clipping level tuned to the target accuracy, and a phased adaptive scheme that matches the clipping level to the current statistical scale. Finally, we prove a _K_-arm equal-gap lower bound showing that the logarithmic penalty is intrinsic to finite-variance 1-bit feedback. It matches the leading _K_, gap, and confidence dependence of the phased upper bound on these worst-case instances, up to lower-order loglog factors.

## 1.1 Problem setting

We study fixed-confidence best-arm identification under 1-bit feedback. The learner is given a finite collection of arms A={1,2_,...,K_}. Pulling arm \(k\in\mathcal{A}\) produces an i.i.d. reward drawn from an unknown distribution \(\nu_k\) on R with mean \(\mu_k:=\mathbb{E}_{X\sim\nu_k}[X]\).

Throughout the paper, we assume that there is a known variance proxy \(\sigma>0\) such that<tbc>

\(\mathrm{Var}_{X\sim\nu_k}(X)\le\sigma^2\text{for all}k\in\mathcal{A}.\)

<tbc>In addition, for each arm _k_ we assume that we are given an anchor point _c<sub>k</sub>_ satisfying

\(|\mu_k-c_k|\le\sigma.\)

We assume that the best arm is unique, and denote it by \(k^\star=\mathrm{argmax}_{k\in\mathcal{A}}\mu_k\), and \(\mu^\star:=\mu_{k^\star}\).

**Remark 1** (Role of assumptions)**.** _The variance bound is the basic moment assumption under which our 1-bit estimator operates. The anchor condition plays a different role: it gives a localization of each arm mean, which is exactly what allows the 1-bit estimator to work efficiently. This localization can itself be obtained by the preliminary 1-bit routine_ MEDIANEST_, using at most_ \(O\left(K\mathrm{log}\frac{K\lambda}{\delta\sigma}\right)\) _threshold queries if_ \(\mu\in[-\lambda,\lambda]\) _with known_ \(\lambda\)_; see Appendix A. Furthermore, while we use_ \(|\mu_k-c_k|\le\sigma\) _for convenience, an anchor distance of_ \(|\mu_k-c_k|\le O(\sigma)\) _is adequate and only alters the constant factors in the bounds, as detailed in the Appendix A._

For every suboptimal arm \(k\neq k^\star\), define the gap \(\Delta_k:=\mu^\star-\mu_k>0\), and for the optimal arm define \(\Delta_{k^\star}:=\mathrm{min}_{j\neq k^\star}\Delta_j\). These gaps quantify the intrinsic difficulty of the instance: small gaps mean that the learner must distinguish arms with very close means, and hence must collect more information before stopping.

### 1-bit interaction model.

The learner does not observe rewards directly. Instead, at round _t_, it chooses an arm \(k_t\in\mathcal{A}\) together with a measurable query set \(A_t\subseteq\mathbb{R}\). The agent then observes a fresh reward sample \(X_{k_t,t}\sim\nu_{k_t}\) and returns only the single bit<tbc>

\(Y_t=\mathbf{1}\{X_{k_t,t}\in A_t\}\in\{0,1\}.\)

Both the arm choice and the query set may depend on the entire past history, so the interaction is fully adaptive. This is the same 1-bit set-query model used in the lower-bound construction. In the algorithmic part of the paper, we only use randomized threshold queries, which form a particularly simple subclass of measurable set queries.

### Objective.

Fix an accuracy parameter \(\varepsilon>0\). We define the set of \(\varepsilon\)-optimal arms by

\(A_\varepsilon(\nu):=\{k\in\mathcal{A}:\mu_k\ge\mu^\star-\varepsilon\}.\)

A 1-bit best-arm identification algorithm consists of an adaptive query strategy, a stopping time \(\tau\), and a recommendation \(\widehat{k}\in\mathcal{A}\). It is said to be \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-PAC if \(Pr_\nu(\tau<\infty)=1\) and \(Pr_\nu\big(\widehat{k}\notin A_\varepsilon(\nu)\big)\le\delta\) for every bandit instance \(\nu=(\nu_1,\dots,\nu_K)\) satisfying the above assumptions. Equivalently, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), the output arm satisfies \(\mu_\widehat{k}\ge\mu^\star-\varepsilon\).

This \(\varepsilon\)-relaxed objective is natural in our setting. It allows the learner to stop once it has ruled out all arms that are worse than the optimum by more than \(\varepsilon\), without spending additional samples to separate nearly tied arms. In particular, when \(\varepsilon<\Delta_{k^\star}\), the set \(A_\varepsilon(\nu)\) reduces to {_k<sup>⋆</sup>_}, and the \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-PAC requirement becomes exact best-arm identification.

## 1.2 Contributions

### A time-uniform 1-bit mean-estimation primitive for adaptive BAI.

In Section 2, we formulate a randomized-threshold mean-estimation primitive based on a clipped tail-integral identity (Lemma 2). The resulting estimator admits confidence sequences that are valid uniformly over time (Theorem 5), which is essential for BAI because the number of samples collected from each arm is random and data-dependent. As a standalone mean estimator, its sample complexity matches the optimal finite- variance 1-bit mean-estimation rate of Lau and Scarlett \[21\], up to the standard iterated-logarithmic price of time-uniform validity (Corollary 6). The contribution here is structural rather than rate-level: rather than improving the standalone mean-estimation rate, we provide a BAI-ready confidence sequence that remains valid under adaptive arm selection and stopping.

### Fixed-confidence BAI algorithms under 1-bit feedback.

In Section 3, we show how to turn the above primitive into fixed-confidence BAI algorithms. The first algorithm, FIXEDCLIP-1BITBAI, uses a single clipping level tuned to the target accuracy \(\varepsilon\). It is simple and fully anytime, but its sample complexity contains an additional mixed term caused by the range of the clipped 1-bit statistic (Theorem 8). The second algorithm, RESTARTPHASEDCLIP-1BITBAI, uses phased adaptive clipping: it proceeds from coarse to fine resolutions and chooses the clipping level according to the current resolution. This removes the fixed-clipping mixed term and yields the main gap-adaptive upper bound of the paper (Theorem 10). Both algorithms are \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-PAC, and their sample complexities are compared in Subsection 3.3.

### A matching information-theoretic lower bound for 1-bit BAI.

In Section 4, we prove a worst- case lower bound for fixed-confidence BAI under 1-bit set queries. The construction is closely related in spirit to multiscale hard instances for finite-variance 1-bit mean estimation of Lau and Scarlett \[21\], but is formulated directly as a _K_-arm BAI lower bound and combined with a change-of-measure argument for adaptive stopping. For a _K_-arm instance with all suboptimal gaps equal to \(\Delta\), we show that any algorithm that is \(\delta\)-correct over the instance class must have an expected stopping time of at least \(\Omega\left((K-1)\frac{\sigma^2}{\Delta^2}log\frac{\sigma}{\Delta}log\frac{1}{\delta}\right)\) (Theorem 12). This demonstrates that the \(\Theta(log\frac{\sigma}{\Delta})\) penalty is an unavoidable consequence of the 1-bit feedback constraint, proving that our algorithm is asymptotically optimal up to a loglog factor.

### Empirical validation.

Section 5 evaluates our 1-bit mean estimator and best-arm identification algorithms. For standalone estimation, our randomized estimator achieves lower mean absolute error and a smaller bias floor than the finite-variance baseline of Lau and Scarlett \[21\]. In the tested bandit settings, phased adaptive clipping uses fewer queries than fixed clipping on instances with heterogeneous gaps.

In the remainder of this paper, the main text presents and discusses our primary theoretical and numerical results, while all formal proofs, detailed algorithms, and experimental configurations are deferred to the appendix.

### 1.3 Related work

#### Fixed-confidence best-arm identification.

The fixed-confidence PAC framework for bandits and foundational sample-complexity lower bounds for pure exploration were developed in \[6, 22\]. A large subsequent literature developed gap-adaptive algorithms and instance-dependent complexity measures, including successive elimination methods \[14\], LUCB-style subset-selection algorithms \[13\], UGapE-type candidate-challenger algorithms \[7\], and time-uniform confidence methods such as lil’UCB \[12\]. Information-theoretic lower bounds and asymptotically optimal sampling rules were developed in \[15, 8\]. The closest algorithmic template to ours is the UGapE framework of Gabillon et al. \[7\], which compares a candidate arm against its strongest challenger using confidence intervals. All of these works assume direct access to the realized reward at each round, so empirical means and confidence intervals can be formed directly; our setting drops this assumption.

#### Quantized feedback and communication-limited learning.

Communication limits have motivated a broad line of work on statistical inference and learning from quantized or few-bit messages \[4, 2, 3, 24\]. A particularly relevant subproblem is mean estimation from compressed, distributed, or one-bit observations \[16, 5, 18, 1\]. In bandit problems, limited communication has been studied in regret minimization and distributed exploration settings \[25, 10, 11\]. Our setting differs in that the objective is fixed-confidence best-arm identification, the feedback consists of adaptive one-bit set queries, and the rewards are only assumed to have finite variance. This weak moment assumption is what forces clipping and leads to the logarithmic penalty analyzed in this paper.

#### 1-bit mean estimation and threshold queries.

The fundamental statistical task underlying our approach is estimating the mean of a real-valued distribution from binary threshold comparisons. Lau and Scarlett \[21\] recently established order-optimal rates for this problem in the finite-variance regime, achieving the sample complexity \(O((\sigma^2/\beta^2)log(\sigma/\beta)log(1/\gamma))\); crucially, they show that the \(log(\sigma/\beta)\) factor is unavoidable with only a second-moment assumption, since the distribution need not have known bounded support. Our 1-bit estimator matches this rate up to the loglog overhead of time-uniform validity, and our lower bound shows that the same \(log(\sigma/\Delta)\) penalty transfers directly to the BAI problem. In contrast to standalone mean estimation, fixed-confidence BAI requires confidence guarantees that remain valid under adaptive arm selection, elimination, and stopping. Thus, the role of our randomized-threshold primitive is not to improve the standalone mean-estimation rate, but to provide an anytime confidence sequence that can be embedded directly into candidate-challenger BAI algorithms. The 1-bit framework also connects to the quantile bandit setting \[19\], which uses 1-bit feedback to identify the arm with the best quantile rather than the best mean.

## 2 A 1-bit mean estimator

We develop the 1-bit mean-estimation primitive through a three-stage construction. First, we establish a tail-integral identity that expresses the mean of a clipped variable as an integral of threshold probabilities. Second, we introduce a randomized thresholding scheme that allows us to estimate this integral using only a single bit per sample while maintaining a controlled bias-variance tradeoff. Finally, we derive a time-uniform confidence sequence for the mean, which enables the estimator to be used in adaptive, data-dependent stopping rules. We also discuss the sample complexity of the estimator in Corollary 6, and compare with the baseline of \[21\] in Remark 7.

Fix one arm and suppress the arm index. Let _X_ have mean \(\mu\), variance at most \(\sigma^2\), and let _c_ be an anchor point satisfying \(|\mu-c|\le\sigma\). Define the centered variable _W_:=_X-c_. Then

\(\mathbb{E}[W]=\mu-c,\mathbb{E}[W^2]\le Var(W)+(\mathbb{E}[W])^2\le 2\sigma^2.\)

Thus _W_ has controlled second moment and is centered near zero. Our task is now to estimate E\[_W_\], and hence \(\mu\), using only 1-bit threshold information.

## 2.1 A tail-integral identity

The starting point is an identity that rewrites a clipped value in terms of tail events. For _L\>_0, define

\([w]_L:=\left\{\begin{array}{ c c }
-L, & w<-L, \\
w, & -L\le w\le L, \\
L, & w>L.
\end{array}\right.\)

The point of clipping is that it separates the estimation problem into two parts: a bounded quantity, which can be estimated reliably, and a bias term, which we will control using the variance bound.

**Lemma 2** (Tail-integral identity)**.** _For every_ \(w\in\mathbb{R}\) _and every L\>_0,

\([w]_L=\int_0^L\left(\mathbf{1}\{w\ge t\}-\mathbf{1}\{w\le-t\}\right)dt.\)

_Consequently,_ \(\mathbb{E}[[W]_L]=\int_0^L\left(Pr(W\ge t)-Pr(W\le-t)\right)dt\).

This identity is the bridge between mean estimation and 1-bit queries. It says that the clipped-variable mean can be written as an integral of differences between upper-tail and lower-tail probabilities. Since each of those probabilities can be accessed through a threshold comparison, the identity suggests that we should estimate the integral by randomizing the threshold _t_ and asking only a single yes/no question per sample. The proof is given in Appendix B.1.

## 2.2 A 1-bit randomized estimator

To turn the tail-integral identity into an estimator, we need a distribution over _t_. For \(L\ge\sigma\), define

\(\alpha_L:=1+log\frac{L}{\sigma},g_L(t):=\frac{1}{\alpha_Lmax\{\sigma,t\}},t\in[0,L].\)

Then _g<sub>L</sub>_ is a density on \[0_,L_\], since \(\int_0^Lg_L(t)dt=\alpha_L^{-1}\left(\int_0^\sigma dt/\sigma+\int_\sigma^Ldt/t\right)=1\).

The shape of _g<sub>L</sub>_ is important. It places relatively more mass on small thresholds _t_, where the query is informative, while still assigning enough mass to larger thresholds to represent the integral up to _L_.

### Randomized query and estimator.

Draw \(S\in\{+1,-1\}\) uniformly, independently of everything else, and draw _T∼g<sub>L</sub>_. Given a fresh reward sample _X_, issue the 1-bit query<tbc>

\(Y=\mathbf{1}\{S(X-c)\ge T\}.\)

<tbc>Equivalently, when _S_=+1 we ask whether \(X\ge c+T\), and when _S_=-1 we ask whether \(X\le c-T\). We then define

\(Z:=\frac{2S}{g_L(T)}Y.\)

The next lemma summarizes why this construction works.

**Lemma 3** (Unbiasedness, variance, and range)**.** _For every_ \(L\ge\sigma\):

_(i)_ \(\mathbb{E}[Z]=\mathbb{E}[[W]_L]\), _(ii)_ \(Var(Z)\le 3\alpha_L\sigma^2\)_, (iii)_ \(|Z|\le 2\alpha_LL\) _almost surely._

Each part of the lemma has a different role. The first part shows that _Z_ is exactly unbiased for the clipped-variable mean. The second part gives a variance bound of the correct scale, up to the logarithmic factor \(\alpha_L\). The third part provides an almost-sure range bound. Together, the second and third parts are precisely what is needed to apply Bernstein’s inequality; the proof is given in Appendix B.2.

Of course, _Z_ is unbiased only for the clipped-variable mean E\[\[_W_\]_<sub>L</sub>_\], not for E\[_W_\] itself. The next lemma quantifies the price paid for clipping.

**Lemma 4** (Clipping bias)**.** _For every_ \(L\ge\sigma\),

\(\left|\mathbb{E}[W]-\mathbb{E}[[W]_L]\right|\le\frac{\sigma^2}{2L}.\)

This bound has the expected form: increasing the clipping level _L_ reduces the bias, but making _L_ too large will worsen the variance bound \(3\alpha_L\sigma^2\) as well as the range bound \(2\alpha_LL\). The estimator therefore has a standard bias-variance tradeoff, and the choice of _L_ needs to balance the two effects. The bias proof is given in Appendix B.3.

### 2.3 Confidence sequence for the tail-integral estimator

Let _Z_<sub>1</sub>_,Z_<sub>2</sub>_,..._ be i.i.d. copies of the above estimator, each built from an independent reward sample and independent internal randomization. Define

\(\bar{Z}_n:=\frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^nZ_i,\hat{\mu}_n:=c+\bar{Z}_n.\)

Since \(\bar{Z}_n\) estimates the clipped-variable mean and _c_ restores the shift, \(\hat{\mu}_n\) is our 1-bit estimate of \(\mu\).

**Theorem 5** (Confidence sequence for the tail-integral estimator)**.** _For every_ \(L\ge\sigma\) _and_ \(\gamma\in(0,1)\)_, with probability at least_ \(1-\gamma,|\hat{\mu}_n-\mu|\le\beta(n,\gamma,L)\) _for all_ \(n\ge 1\)_, where_

\(\beta(n,\gamma,L)=\frac{\sigma^2}{2L}+2\sqrt{\frac{3\alpha_L\sigma^2x_n(\gamma)}{n}}+\frac{\alpha_LLx_n(\gamma)}{n},\)

_with_ \(\alpha_L=1+\mathrm{log}(L/\sigma)\) _and_ \(x_n(\gamma):=\mathrm{log}\big(\pi^2(1+\lfloor\mathrm{log}_2n\rfloor)^2/(3\gamma)\big)\).

The first term in \(\beta(n,\gamma,L)\) is the clipping bias, the second is the main stochastic fluctuation term, and the third is the Bernstein range correction. The only price paid for time-uniformity is the stitched penalty \(x_n(\gamma)\), which is of order \(\mathrm{log}(1/\gamma)+\mathrm{loglog}(e+n)\). The proof of Theorem 5 is in Appendix B.4, and the sample-complexity inversion below is proved in Appendix B.5.

**Corollary 6** (Sample complexity of the tail-integral estimator)**.** _Fix a target accuracy_ \(\beta\in(0,\sigma)\) _and an error probability_ \(\gamma\in(0,1/3)\)_. By setting the clipping level_ \(L=\frac{2\sigma^2}{\beta}\)_, the tail-integral estimator_ \(\hat{\mu}_n\) _satisfies_ \(|\hat{\mu}_n-\mu|\le\beta\) _with probability at least_ \(1-\gamma\) _for sample sizes n satisfying:_

\(n=O\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{\beta^2}\mathrm{log}\frac{\sigma}{\beta}\left[\mathrm{log}\frac{1}{\gamma}+\mathrm{loglog}\left(e+\frac{\sigma}{\beta}\right)\right]\right).\)

**Remark 7** (Comparison with \[21\])**.** _In the finite-variance regime, \[21\] achieve the optimal rate_ \(O\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{\beta^2}\mathrm{log}\frac{\sigma}{\beta}\mathrm{log}\frac{1}{\gamma}\right)\)_. Our estimator matches this rate up to the lower-order_ loglog _factor needed for time-uniform validity. Structurally, their estimator partitions the domain into geometric regions and assigns fixed regional budgets, whereas ours samples a single randomized threshold from g<sub>L</sub> and yields an anytime confidence sequence. This avoids fixed regional allocations and makes the estimator compatible with adaptive bandit sampling and stopping rules._

## 3 1-bit BAI algorithm and upper bound

We now convert the time-uniform 1-bit mean confidence sequence from Section 2 into fixed- confidence BAI algorithms. Our algorithms follow the candidate-challenger interval logic of \[7\]. At each time, we construct arm-wise confidence intervals, select a candidate arm _h_, identify its strongest challenger \(\ell\), and stop once the candidate is certified to be \(\varepsilon\)-optimal. If the stopping condition is not met, the algorithm samples the more uncertain arm among \(\{h,\ell\}\), namely the one with the larger confidence radius.

The main new difficulty, compared with the unquantized setting, is the choice of the clipping level _L_. A larger clipping level reduces the bias of the 1-bit mean estimator but increases both its variance factor and its range term. Thus, the clipping level must be matched to the statistical resolution at which arms are being compared.

We present two approaches. The first is a fixed-clipping algorithm, which chooses a single clipping level tuned to the target accuracy \(\varepsilon\). This algorithm is simple and fully anytime, but it pays an additional mixed term in the sample complexity; see Theorem 8. The second is a phased adaptive- clipping algorithm, which gradually decreases the statistical resolution and chooses the clipping level accordingly. This removes the mixed term and yields the main gap-adaptive upper bound of the paper; see Theorem 10. Both algorithms are \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)-PAC, and their sample complexities are compared in Subsection 3.3.

Consider the non-trivial case \(0<\varepsilon\le\sigma\); the case \(\varepsilon>\sigma\) is trivial up to constants and can be handled by the initial phase alone. Define \(\widetilde{\Delta}_k:=\mathrm{max}\{\Delta_k,\varepsilon\}\), and \(\overline{\Delta_k}:=\mathrm{min}\{\widetilde{\Delta}_k,\sigma\}\).

## 3.1 Fixed clipping bias

The simplest implementation chooses the clipping level from the target accuracy:<tbc>

\(L_\varepsilon:=\frac{2\sigma^2}{\varepsilon},\alpha_\varepsilon:=1+log\frac{L_\varepsilon}{\sigma}=1+log\frac{2\sigma}{\varepsilon}.\)

<tbc>By Lemma 4, the clipping bias is at most \(\varepsilon/4\). The confidence radius from Theorem 5 becomes

\(\beta_\varepsilon(n,\gamma)=\frac{\varepsilon}{4}+2\sqrt{\frac{3\alpha_\varepsilon\sigma^2x_n(\gamma)}{n}}+\frac{2\alpha_\varepsilon\sigma^2x_n(\gamma)}{n\varepsilon}.\)

Algorithm FIXEDCLIP-1BITBAI uses this radius with \(\gamma=\delta/K\). At each round it forms confidence intervals \[LCB_<sub>k</sub>,_UCB_<sub>k</sub>_\] of \(\mu_k\), sets \(B_k=max_{a\neq k}\mathrm{UCB}_a-\mathrm{LCB}_k\), lets \(h\in argmin_kB_k\) and \(\ell\in argmax_{a\neq h}\mathrm{UCB}_a\), stops if \(B_h\le\varepsilon\), and otherwise samples the more uncertain arm in \(\{h,\ell\}\) using the 1-bit tail-integral query at clipping level \(L_\varepsilon\). Detailed pseudocode is given in Algorithm 3 in Appendix E.

From the expression of \(\beta_\varepsilon(n,\gamma)\), the sample requirement is no longer governed only by the usual _n_<sup>-1/2</sup> concentration term. In addition, there is a lower-order \(n^{-1}\varepsilon^{-1}\) term coming from the Bernstein range correction. This term is a direct consequence of the clipping level \(L_\varepsilon\) chosen so that the clipping bias is at most \(\varepsilon/4\), affecting the final sample complexity. This leads to the hardness quantity:

\(H_\mathrm{fix}(\varepsilon):=\alpha_\varepsilon\sum_{k=1}^K\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{\widetilde{\Delta}_k^2}+\frac{\sigma^2}{\varepsilon\widetilde{\Delta}_k}\right).\)

With this hardness quantity, we can state the sample complexity upper bound.

**Theorem 8** (Fixed clipping upper bound)**.** FIXEDCLIP-1BITBAI _is_ \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)_-PAC. With probability at least_ \(1-\delta\)_, its needed number of 1-bit queries satisfies_

\(N_\mathrm{fix}=O\big(H_\mathrm{fix}(\varepsilon)\left[log\frac{K}{\delta}+loglogH_\mathrm{fix}(\varepsilon)\right]\big).\)

The proof of Theorem 8 is given in Appendix C.1. A finite deterministic query bound also holds on every realization for \(\varepsilon>0\), guaranteeing termination even outside the confidence event; together with interval correctness this establishes the PAC guarantee. The deterministic bound and proof are given in Appendix C.3.1.

**Remark 9** (The choice of clipping level _L_)**.** _The fixed choice_ \(L_\varepsilon=2\sigma^2/\varepsilon\) _is simple and ensures bias at most_ \(\varepsilon/4\)_, but it is not instance-optimal, especially when_ \(\varepsilon\checkmark\Delta_k\) _or_ \(\varepsilon=0\)_. For exact best-arm identification_ \(\varepsilon=0\)_, the natural scale is_ \(L_\star=\Theta(\sigma^2/\Delta_{k^\star})\)_; more generally, the oracle arm-wise choice would be_ \(L_k=\Theta(\sigma^2/\widetilde{\Delta}_k)\)_, leading to the gap-adaptive hardness_

\(H_\mathrm{gap}=\sum_{k=1}^K\left(1+log\frac{\sigma}{\overline{\Delta_k}}\right)\frac{\sigma^2}{\overline{\Delta_k^2}}.\)

The phased algorithm below obtains this behavior without knowing the gaps.

## 3.2 Phased adaptive clipping

The intuition behind the phased algorithm is that easy arms should not be estimated at the finest accuracy scale. In FIXEDCLIP-1BITBAI, the clipping level is fixed using the target accuracy \(\varepsilon\), so even an arm with a large gap pays the range cost associated with resolving \(\varepsilon\)-level differences. The phased algorithm instead proceeds from coarse to fine resolutions. At phase _j_, it uses a clipping level matched to the current resolution \(\rho_j\) and eliminates arms that are already distinguishable at that scale. Only statistically competitive arms survive to finer phases. This removes the fixed-clipping mixed term and yields a bound depending on each arm’s own effective gap.

To implement this idea, schedule resolutions<tbc>

\(\rho_j:=2^{-j}\sigma,J:=\lceil log_2(\sigma/\varepsilon)\rceil,j=0,1,\dots,J,\)

and at phase _j_ set \(L_j:=32\sigma^2/\rho_j\), \(\alpha_j:=1+log(32\sigma/\rho_j)\), and \(r_j:=\rho_j/16\). With \(\gamma=\delta/[K(J+1)]\),

\(\beta_j(n)=\frac{\rho_j}{64}+2\sqrt{\frac{3\alpha_j\sigma^2x_n(\gamma)}{n}}+\frac{32\alpha_j\sigma^2x_n(\gamma)}{\rho_jn}.\)

The choice of _L<sub>j</sub>_ makes the clipping bias of phase _j_ at most \(\rho_j/64\), while \(r_j=\rho_j/16\) is the target statistical radius at that resolution. Thus, phase _j_ should be viewed as a test of whether the currently active arms can already be separated at scale \(\rho_j\). If the confidence intervals are still too wide, the algorithm continues sampling; if all active arms have confidence radius at most _r<sub>j</sub>_, then arms that are clearly suboptimal at this scale can be safely removed.

Algorithm RESTARTPHASEDCLIP-1BITBAI implements this idea using fresh estimators at every phase; detailed pseudocode is given in Algorithm 4 in Appendix E. Within phase _j_, it adaptively samples active arms until either some arm is certified to be \(\varepsilon\)-optimal or all active arms have confidence radius at most _r<sub>j</sub>_. ## 3.3 Discussion of the sample complexity

### Fixed clipping vs Phased clipping.

The fixed method is simpler and fully anytime, but it pays the mixed term \(\sigma^2/(\varepsilon\widetilde{\Delta}_k)\) because the range of the 1-bit statistic is proportional to \(L_\varepsilon=\Theta(\sigma^2/\varepsilon)\). This term is unavoidable for a globally fixed clipping level, but it is wasteful for arms with \(\Delta_k\gg\varepsilon\). The phased method matches _L<sub>j</sub>_ to the current resolution \(\rho_j\), so the range term is balanced at the scale where the arm is actually distinguished; its cost is essentially \((1+log(\sigma/\overline{\Delta_k}))\sigma^2/\overline{\Delta_k^2}\) per arm.

### Compared with unquantized fixed-confidence BAI.

The distribution-free hardness of unquantized BAI is \(\sum_k\sigma^2/\widetilde{\Delta}_k^2\) (\[7\]), 1-bit feedback introduces the additional logarithmic factor \(1+log(\sigma/\overline{\Delta_k})\) in the phased bound. The lower bound in Section 4 shows that this logarithmic penalty is inevitable in the finite-variance regime.

### Lau-Scarlett \[21\] with phased successive elimination.

At each resolution \(\rho_j\), run their fixed- target estimator on each active arm with accuracy \(\rho_j/8\) and confidence \(1-\delta/[K(J+1)]\), then retain estimates within \(\rho_j/2\) of the maximum. Simultaneous confidence control yields total cost \(O(H_\mathrm{gap}log(K(J+1)/\delta))\), matching our leading rate. Appendix C.4 gives the correctness and counting argument.

### Total sample complexity.

If the anchors are not initially available but the means lie in \([-\lambda,\lambda]\), running MEDIANEST for each arm adds an additional \(O\big(K(log\frac{\lambda}{\sigma}+log\frac{K}{\delta})\big)\) term to the sample complexity, which does not scale with \(\varepsilon\) or the gaps \(\Delta_k\).

## 4 Lower bound

We now establish an information-theoretic lower bound for fixed-confidence best-arm identification under 1-bit set queries. The construction is closely related in spirit to the multiscale hard instances that arise in finite-variance 1-bit mean estimation \[21\]: in both settings, one-bit queries cannot avoid a logarithmic loss under only a second-moment assumption. Here, we formulate this obstruction directly in the BAI setting by embedding opposite perturbations of a multiscale one-dimensional distribution into a _K_-arm instance and combining it with a change-of-measure argument for adaptive stopping. The construction uses a symmetric distribution _P_<sub>0</sub> of mean zero and perturbed distributions _P_<sub>-</sub> and _P_<sub>+</sub> of means \(-\Delta\) and \(+\Delta\).

The base instance (_P_<sub>0</sub>_,P_<sub>-</sub>_,...,P_<sub>-</sub>) has _K_-1 equal suboptimal gaps \(\Delta\). For each \(i\ge 2\), changing only arm _i_ to _P_<sub>+</sub> changes the best arm to _i_. A change of measure forces sufficient queries to each such arm under the same base instance, and summing gives the factor _K_-1.

**Theorem 12** (_K_-arm worst-case lower bound for 1-bit BAI)**.** _Fix_ \(K\ge 2\), \(\sigma>0\), \(\delta\in(0,1/4)\)_, and_ \(\Delta\in(0,\sigma/4]\)_. There exists a K-arm instance_ \(\nu^{(0)}\) _with variance at most_ \(\sigma^2\) _for every arm and all suboptimal gaps equal to_ \(\Delta\)_, such that every 1-bit algorithm that is_ \(\delta\)_-correct for exact BAI over the stated instance class satisfies_

\(\mathbb{E}_{\nu^{(0)}}[\tau]\ge c(K-1)\frac{\sigma^2}{\Delta^2}\mathrm{log}\frac{\sigma}{\Delta}\mathrm{log}\frac{1}{\delta}\)

_for an absolute constant c\>_0_. The same bound holds for algorithms that are_ \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)_-PAC over this class when_ \(0<\varepsilon<\Delta/2\).

All base and alternative distributions admit the same anchor _c<sub>k</sub>_=0, so the bound persists when valid anchors are supplied. The construction, uniform one-query KL bound, and adaptive change- of-measure proof appear in Appendices D.1-D.3. On the equal-gap base instance, \(H_\mathrm{gap}=K(1+\mathrm{log}(\sigma/\Delta))\sigma^2/\Delta^2\). When \(\delta\le 1/K\), \(\mathrm{log}(1/\delta)\) and \(\mathrm{log}(K/\delta)\) are equivalent up to constants. Hence the expected lower bound matches the leading _K_, gap, and confidence dependence of the high- probability phased upper bound, up to lower-order iterated logarithms. This worst-case comparison does not characterize the optimal expected complexity on every instance.

## 6 Conclusion

We introduced a fixed-confidence best-arm identification framework for finite-variance, 1-bit feedback environments. Using a novel randomized-threshold mean estimator, we developed a baseline fixed- clipping algorithm alongside a gap-adaptive phased alternative which achieves worst-case optimality up to loglog factors. Addressing current limitations offers clear avenues for future work. First, our algorithms rely on an localization assumption; developing methods that weaken or remove this requirement is an important next step. Second, our analysis currently relies on a K-arm worst-case lower bound, leaving the exact instance-dependent complexity of 1-bit BAI open. Finally, extending our time-uniform 1-bit primitive to broader pure-exploration tasks presents an exciting direction for communication-constrained learning.

### A.1 Bounding the mean via the median

In Section 2, we assumed that for each arm _k_, the learner is provided with an anchor point _c<sub>k</sub>_ satisfying \(|\mu_k-c_k|\le\sigma\). We can rigorously satisfy this assumption by estimating the median of the reward distribution.

Let _c_ be the true median of a random variable _X_ with mean \(\mu\) and variance bounded by \(\sigma^2\). By Cantelli’s inequality (the one-sided Chebyshev inequality), for any _a\>_0, we have:<tbc>

\(Pr(X-\mu\ge a)\le\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+a^2}.\)

<tbc>If the median is greater than the mean (\(c>\mu\)), we can substitute \(a=c-\mu\) to obtain:<tbc>

\(Pr(X\ge c)\le\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+(c-\mu)^2}.\)

<tbc>By the definition of the median, \(Pr(X\ge c)\ge\frac{1}{2}\). Combining these yields:

\(\frac{1}{2}\le\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+(c-\mu)^2}\Longrightarrow\sigma^2+(c-\mu)^2\le 2\sigma^2\Longrightarrow(c-\mu)^2\le\sigma^2.\)

Taking the square root gives \(|c-\mu|\le\sigma\). A symmetric argument using \(Pr(X\le c)\) applies when \(c<\mu\). Therefore, finding a point close to the true median naturally provides a valid anchor point _c<sub>k</sub>_ that is guaranteed to be at most \(O(\sigma)\) away from the true mean.

## A.4 Parameter selection and estimate validity

### Choosing the Tolerance (\(\varepsilon'\)).

Because the sample complexity \(M(n,\varepsilon',\gamma)\) scales aggressively as \(O(1/(\varepsilon')^2)\), we cannot afford to let \(\varepsilon'\) shrink to 0 alongside the main BAI target accuracy \(\varepsilon\). Instead, we fix \(\varepsilon'\) as a moderate constant by setting \(\varepsilon'=0.05\). This choice avoids an exploding sample cost while maintaining a strictly bounded localization window.

### Choosing the Grid Density (_n_).

Discretize the bounded domain \([-\lambda,\lambda]\) using a uniform step size \(\Delta x=\kappa\cdot\sigma\) for a small constant \(\kappa>0\). This results in a grid of size \(n=\Theta(\lambda/\sigma)\). Crucially, because _n_ appears inside a logarithm in the sample complexity \(M(n,\varepsilon',\gamma)\), this domain discretization contributes only an additive logarithmic term to the sample budget. The following lemma transforms the probability guarantees of MEDIANEST into rigorous bounds of the distance to the true mean.

**Lemma 13** (Estimate Validity via MEDIANEST)**.** _Let X be a random variable with mean_ \(\mu\in[-\lambda,\lambda]\) _and variance proxy_ \(\sigma^2\)_. Let the continuous domain_ \([-\lambda,\lambda]\) _be discretized into a uniform grid with step size_ \(\Delta x=\kappa\cdot\sigma\)_. If the_ MEDIANEST _routine successfully identifies an_ \(\varepsilon'\)_-good interval_ \[_x<sub>i</sub>,x_<sub>_i_+1</sub>\] _for the target_ \(\tau=1/2\)_, then the returned midpoint_ \(\widehat{c}=(x_i+x_{i+1})/2\) _satisfies:_<tbc>

\(|\widehat{c}-\mu|\le\left(\sqrt{\frac{1/2+\varepsilon'}{1/2-\varepsilon'}}+\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)\sigma.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ Because the returned interval is \(\varepsilon'\)-good, the probability range \([Pr(X\le x_i),Pr(X\le x_{i+1})]\) must intersect the target window \((1/2-\varepsilon',1/2+\varepsilon')\). Since cumulative probabilities are non- decreasing, this intersection gives us two conditions:

\(Pr(X\le x_i)<\frac{1}{2}+\varepsilon'\text{and}Pr(X\le x_{i+1})>\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon'\)

We can use these to bound the tails. The upper tail satisfies \(Pr(X>x_i)=1-Pr(X\le x_i)>1/2-\varepsilon'\), while the lower tail directly satisfies \(Pr(X\le x_{i+1})>1/2-\varepsilon'\). We evaluate the distance from \(\mu\) to the grid step by considering three cases:

**Case 1 (**\(\mu<x_i\)**):** Applying Cantelli’s inequality gives \(Pr(X\ge x_i)\le\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+(x_i-\mu)^2}\). Combining with our known tail bound, we get:<tbc>

\(\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon'<Pr(X>x_i)\le Pr(X\ge x_i)\le\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+(x_i-\mu)^2}\)

<tbc>Solving for the distance yields \(x_i-\mu<\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1/2+\varepsilon'}{1/2-\varepsilon'}}\). Because the returned estimate \(\widehat{c}\) is the midpoint of the grid interval, its distance to the true mean is<tbc>

\(|\widehat{c}-\mu|=\frac{\Delta x}{2}+(x_i-\mu)<\frac{\kappa\sigma}{2}+\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1/2+\varepsilon'}{1/2-\varepsilon'}}.\)

<tbc>**Case 2 (**\(\mu>x_{i+1}\)**):** Applying a symmetric Cantelli bound gives \(Pr(X\le x_{i+1})\le\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+(\mu-x_{i+1})^2}\). Combining with our lower tail condition, we have:<tbc>

\(\frac{1}{2}-\varepsilon'<Pr(X\le x_{i+1})\le\frac{\sigma^2}{\sigma^2+(\mu-x_{i+1})^2}\)

<tbc>Rearranging the inequality yields \(\mu-x_{i+1}<\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1/2+\varepsilon'}{1/2-\varepsilon'}}\). The distance from the midpoint is

\(|\widehat{c}-\mu|=(\mu-x_{i+1})+\frac{\Delta x}{2}<\sigma\sqrt{\frac{1/2+\varepsilon'}{1/2-\varepsilon'}}+\frac{\kappa\sigma}{2}.\)

**Case 3 (**\(x_i\le\mu\le x_{i+1}\)**):** The true mean is inside the identified interval. The absolute maximum distance from the midpoint \(\widehat{c}\) to any point inside this grid step is trivially bounded by half the step size, \(\frac{\Delta x}{2}=\frac{\kappa\sigma}{2}\) . This is strictly smaller than the bounds derived in Cases 1 and 2.

We conclude that in all possible scenarios, the initial estimate satisfies:

\(|\widehat{c}-\mu|\le\left(\sqrt{\frac{1/2+\varepsilon'}{1/2-\varepsilon'}}+\frac{\kappa}{2}\right)\sigma\)

With \(\varepsilon'=0.05\) and \(\kappa=0.2\), the guaranteed bound becomes \(|\widehat{c}-\mu|\le 1.205\sigma\). We can, in principle, choose \(\varepsilon'\) and \(\kappa\) to bring this bound arbitrarily close to \(\sigma\), but doing so will negatively affect the sample complexity. Because the sample requirement of the MEDIANEST routine scales as \(O(1/(\varepsilon')^2)\) and logarithmically with the grid size \(n\propto 1/\kappa\), shrinking these parameters heavily inflates the initialization cost. Ultimately, pushing for this precision is unnecessary; a difference of \(O(\sigma)\) in the anchor’s distance from the mean will only affect the constant factors in the estimator’s time-uniform confidence sequence (Theorem 5) and the final best-arm identification sample complexity bounds (Theorem 8 and Theorem 10).

**Lemma 14** (Total Initialization Complexity)**.** _By applying a union bound over the K arms and allocating a failure budget of_ \(\gamma=\delta/(2K)\) _to each_ MEDIANEST _instance, the total initialization burn-in phase is bounded by:_<tbc>

\(T_{init}=O\left(K\left(log\frac{\lambda}{\sigma}+log\frac{K}{\delta}\right)\right).\)

<tbc>_Proof._ For each of the _K_ arms, we run the MEDIANEST routine. With our fixed \(\varepsilon'\) and the grid size \(n=\Theta(\lambda/\sigma)\), the sample complexity per arm is bounded by \(M(n,\varepsilon',\delta/(2K))\). The additive terms in the query complexity are:<tbc>

\(O\left(logn+log^{2/3}nlog^{1/3}\frac{1}{\gamma}+log\frac{1}{\gamma}\right).\)

<tbc>By Young’s inequality, the cross term is bounded by the linear combination of the individual logarithmic terms:

\(log^{2/3}nlog^{1/3}\frac{1}{\gamma}\le\frac{2}{3}logn+\frac{1}{3}log\frac{1}{\gamma}=O\left(logn+log\frac{1}{\gamma}\right).\)

Thus, the sample complexity per arm simplifies to \(O\left(logn+log(1/\gamma)\right)\). Substituting \(n=\Theta(\lambda/\sigma)\) and \(\gamma=\delta/(2K)\) yields \(O\left(log\frac{\lambda}{\sigma}+log\frac{K}{\delta}\right)\) samples per arm. Multiplying this per-arm cost by the _K_ parallel instances gives the total bound _T_init. Because _T_init scales strictly with the number of arms _K_ and is entirely independent of the arm gaps \(\Delta_k\), it operates as a purely additive initialization cost.

The key structural step is Lemma 22: whenever the algorithm samples arm _k_, its stochastic radius must still be larger than a constant fraction of the effective gap. ## C.2 Phased adaptive clipping: proof of Theorem 10

We now analyze the restart phased algorithm. We first construct a high-probability event on which all arm-phase confidence intervals are valid simultaneously (Lemma 24). On this event, the elimination and stopping rules never discard the best arm and can only return an \(\varepsilon\)-optimal arm (Lemma 26). The sample complexity analysis then proceeds phase by phase. Lemma 27 gives the number of samples needed to certify a phase-_j_ interval at radius _r<sub>j</sub>_. Lemmas 28 and 29 show that each arm is sampled only down to a resolution comparable to its capped effective gap \(\overline{\Delta_k}\). Summing the resulting dyadic costs over phases and arms gives the claimed bound (Lemma 30).

For each phase \(j=0,1,\dots,J=\lceil log_2(\sigma/\varepsilon)\rceil\), recall<tbc>

\(\rho_j=2^{-j}\sigma,L_j=\frac{32\sigma^2}{\rho_j},r_j=\frac{\rho_j}{16},\alpha_j=1+log\frac{L_j}{\sigma}=1+log\frac{32\sigma}{\rho_j}.\)

<tbc>With \(\gamma=\delta/[K(J+1)]\), the phase-_j_ confidence radius is

\(\beta_j(n)=\frac{\rho_j}{64}+2\sqrt{\frac{3\alpha_j\sigma^2x_n(\gamma)}{n}}+\frac{32\alpha_j\sigma^2x_n(\gamma)}{\rho_jn}.\)

The restart version uses independent fresh estimators in each arm-phase pair (_k,j_).

**Lemma 24** (Phased good event)**.** _With probability at least_ \(1-\delta\)_, the event_

\(\mathcal{E}_\text{ph}:=\cap_{k=1}^K\cap_{j=0}^J\cap_{n\ge 1}\{|\widehat{\mu}_{k,j}(n)-\mu_k|\le\beta_j(n)\}\)

_holds throughout_ RESTARTPHASEDCLIP-1BITBAI.

_Proof._ Fix an arm-phase pair (_k,j_). During phase _j_, the algorithm uses clipping level _L<sub>j</sub>_ for arm _k_. Since<tbc>

\(\frac{\sigma^2}{2L_j}=\frac{\sigma^2}{2\cdot 32\sigma^2/\rho_j}=\frac{\rho_j}{64},\)

<tbc>Theorem 5 with failure probability \(\gamma\) gives<tbc>

\(Pr\left(\forall n\ge 1,|\widehat{\mu}_{k,j}(n)-\mu_k|\le\beta_j(n)\right)\ge 1-\gamma.\)

<tbc>There are _K(J_+1) arm-phase pairs, so the union bound gives

\(Pr(\mathcal{E}_\text{ph})\ge 1-K(J+1)\gamma=1-\delta.\)

Again, the confidence sequence is uniform in the local sample count _n_, so adaptive sampling inside the phase is allowed.

**Lemma 25** (The best arm is never eliminated)**.** _On_ E<sub>ph</sub>, RESTARTPHASEDCLIP-1BITBAI _never eliminates k<sup>⋆</sup>._

_Proof._ Fix a phase _j_ and suppose _k<sup>⋆</sup>_ is active when the elimination rule is applied. Let _A_ be the active set at that moment and let<tbc>

\(m:=max_{i\in A}\mathrm{LCB}_{i,j}.\)

<tbc>On E<sub>ph</sub>, for every active arm _i_,<tbc>

\(\mathrm{LCB}_{i,j}\le\mu_i\le\mu^\star.\)

<tbc>Therefore<tbc>

\(m=max_{i\in A}\mathrm{LCB}_{i,j}\le\mu^\star.\)

<tbc>Also, since _k<sup>⋆</sup>_ is active and its interval is valid,<tbc>

\(\mathrm{UCB}_{k^\star,j}\ge\mu^\star.\)

<tbc>Combining the two displays gives

\(\mathrm{UCB}_{k^\star,j}\ge\mu^\star\ge m>m-\varepsilon.\)

Thus _k<sup>⋆</sup>_ cannot satisfy the elimination condition \(\mathrm{UCB}_{k,j}<m-\varepsilon\).

**Lemma 26** (Phased stopping and final-output correctness)**.** _On_ E<sub>ph</sub>_, every arm returned by_ RESTARTPHASEDCLIP-1BITBAI _is_ \(\varepsilon\)_-optimal._

_Proof._ There are three possible ways the algorithm returns.

_Singleton return._ If the active set has size one, Lemma 25 implies that the unique active arm must be _k<sup>⋆</sup>_, hence the output is correct.

_Interval stopping._ Suppose the algorithm returns an arm _h_ in phase _j_ because, with \(\ell\in argmax_{a\in A\backslash\{h\}}\mathrm{UCB}_{a,j}\),<tbc>

\(\mathrm{UCB}_{\ell,j}-\mathrm{LCB}_{h,j}\le\varepsilon.\)

<tbc>If _h=k<sup>⋆</sup>_, the claim is immediate. Otherwise, Lemma 25 implies that _k<sup>⋆</sup>_ is still active, and since \(k^\star\neq h\),<tbc>

\(\mathrm{UCB}_{\ell,j}=max_{a\in A\backslash\{h\}}\mathrm{UCB}_{a,j}\ge\mathrm{UCB}_{k^\star,j}\ge\mu^\star.\)

<tbc>Also \(\mathrm{LCB}_{h,j}\le\mu_h\), so

\(\mu^\star-\mu_h\le\mathrm{UCB}_{\ell,j}-\mathrm{LCB}_{h,j}\le\varepsilon.\)

Thus _h_ is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.

_Final-phase return._ Finally, suppose the algorithm reaches the final phase _J_ and returns \(h\in argmax_{k\in A}\mathrm{LCB}_{k,J}\) after all active arms satisfy \(\beta_{k,J}\le r_J\). By Lemma 25, _k<sup>⋆</sup>_ is active. Hence<tbc>

\(\mathrm{LCB}_{h,J}\ge\mathrm{LCB}_{k^\star,J}.\)

<tbc>On E<sub>ph</sub> and because \(\beta_{k^\star,J}\le r_J\),<tbc>

\(\mathrm{LCB}_{k^\star,J}=\widehat{\mu}_{k^\star,J}-\beta_{k^\star,J}\ge\mu^\star-2\beta_{k^\star,J}\ge\mu^\star-2r_J.\)

<tbc>Similarly, \(\mu_h\ge\mathrm{LCB}_{h,J}\). Therefore

\(\mu_h\ge\mathrm{LCB}_{h,J}\ge\mathrm{LCB}_{k^\star,J}\ge\mu^\star-2r_J.\)

Since \(r_J=\rho_J/16\) and \(\rho_J\le\varepsilon\), we have \(2r_J\le\varepsilon/8\le\varepsilon\). Thus \(\mu_h\ge\mu^\star-\varepsilon\).

**Lemma 27** (Per-phase sample requirement)**.** _For each phase j, define_<tbc>

\(\Gamma_j:=log\frac{K(J+1)}{\delta}+loglog\left(e^e\frac{\sigma}{\rho_j}\right)+loglog\left(e^e\frac{K(J+1)}{\delta}\right).\)

<tbc>_There exists a universal constant C\>_0 _such that_<tbc>

\(n_j^\circ:=\left[C\frac{\alpha_j\sigma^2}{\rho_j^2}\Gamma_j\right]\)

<tbc>_satisfies_

\(\beta_j(n_j^\circ)\le r_j=\frac{\rho_j}{16}.\)

_Consequently, in phase j, an active arm is queried at most_ \(n_j^\circ\) _times before its phase-j radius is at most r<sub>j</sub>._

_Proof._ Recall<tbc>

\(\beta_j(n)=\frac{\rho_j}{64}+2\sqrt{\frac{3\alpha_j\sigma^2x_n(\gamma)}{n}}+\frac{32\alpha_j\sigma^2x_n(\gamma)}{\rho_jn}.\)

<tbc>The bias term is already \(\rho_j/64\). It remains to make each of the two stochastic terms at most \(\rho_j/64\). First we bound the stitched logarithm at \(n_j^\circ\). Since<tbc>

\(x_n(\gamma)=log\left(\frac{\pi^2(1+\lfloor log_2n\rfloor)^2}{3\gamma}\right),\)

<tbc>there is a universal constant _c_<sub>1</sub>_\>_0 such that for all \(n\ge 2\),<tbc>

\(x_n(\gamma)\le c_1+log\frac{1}{\gamma}+2loglog(e^en).\)

<tbc>Here \(\gamma=\delta/[K(J+1)]\), so<tbc>

\(log\frac{1}{\gamma}=log\frac{K(J+1)}{\delta}.\)

<tbc>Moreover,<tbc>

\(n_j^\circ\le C_1\frac{\alpha_j\sigma^2}{\rho_j^2}\Gamma_j\)

<tbc>for a universal constant _C_<sub>1</sub> depending only on _C_, and<tbc>

\(\alpha_j=1+log\frac{32\sigma}{\rho_j}\le C_2log\left(e^e\frac{\sigma}{\rho_j}\right).\)

<tbc>Therefore<tbc>

\(loglog(e^en_j^\circ)\le C_3+loglog\left(e^e\frac{\sigma}{\rho_j}\right)+loglog\left(e^e\frac{K(J+1)}{\delta}\right),\)

<tbc>where the last term absorbs the dependence on \(\Gamma_j\). Hence, for a universal constant _C_<sub>0</sub>_\>_0,<tbc>

\(x_{n_j^\circ}(\gamma)\le C_0\Gamma_j.\) (7)

<tbc>Now choose the constant _C_ in the definition of \(n_j^\circ\) large enough so that<tbc>

\(2\sqrt{\frac{3\alpha_j\sigma^2C_0\Gamma_j}{n_j^\circ}}\le\frac{\rho_j}{64}\)

<tbc>and<tbc>

\(\frac{32\alpha_j\sigma^2C_0\Gamma_j}{\rho_jn_j^\circ}\le\frac{\rho_j}{64}.\)

<tbc>Using (7), both stochastic terms in \(\beta_j(n_j^\circ)\) are at most \(\rho_j/64\). Thus

\(\beta_j(n_j^\circ)\le\frac{\rho_j}{64}+\frac{\rho_j}{64}+\frac{\rho_j}{64}=\frac{3\rho_j}{64}<\frac{\rho_j}{16}=r_j.\)

In the algorithm, once an arm has \(\beta_{k,j}\le r_j\), it is not queried again in that phase unless all active arms already satisfy the same condition, in which case the phase ends. Therefore an arm receives at most \(n_j^\circ\) phase-_j_ samples.

**Lemma 28** (Elimination at the right scale)**.** _Assume_ E<sub>ph</sub> _holds. Fix a phase j. If a suboptimal active arm_ \(k\neq k^\star\) _satisfies_

\(\Delta_k>\varepsilon+\frac{\rho_j}{4},\)

_then by the time phase j ends, either the algorithm has already stopped or arm k has been eliminated._

_Proof._ If the algorithm stops during phase _j_, there is nothing to prove. Otherwise, phase _j_ ends only after every active arm has phase radius at most \(r_j=\rho_j/16\), and the elimination rule has been applied. Let _A_ be the active set at that point and define<tbc>

\(m:=max_{i\in A}LCB_{i,j}.\)

By Lemma 25, \(k^\star\in A\). Hence, on E<sub>ph</sub>,<tbc>

\(m\ge\mathrm{LCB}_{k^\star,j}\ge\mu^\star-2r_j.\)

<tbc>For the suboptimal arm _k_,<tbc>

\(\mathrm{UCB}_{k,j}\le\mu_k+2r_j=\mu^\star-\Delta_k+2r_j.\)

<tbc>If \(\Delta_k>\varepsilon+4r_j\), then<tbc>

\(\mu^\star-\Delta_k+2r_j<\mu^\star-\varepsilon-2r_j.\)

<tbc>Since \(4r_j=\rho_j/4\), the condition \(\Delta_k>\varepsilon+\rho_j/4\) is exactly \(\Delta_k>\varepsilon+4r_j\). Combining the preceding displays,

\(\mathrm{UCB}_{k,j}<\mu^\star-\varepsilon-2r_j\le m-\varepsilon.\)

Thus _k_ satisfies the elimination rule \(\mathrm{UCB}_{k,j}<m-\varepsilon\) and is eliminated.

**Lemma 29** (Last relevant phase)**.** _Assume_ E<sub>ph</sub> _holds. For every arm k, the resolution of the last phase in which k is sampled is bounded below by a universal constant multiple of_<tbc>

\(\overline{\Delta_k}:=\mathrm{min}\{\mathrm{max}\{\Delta_k,\varepsilon\},\sigma\}.\)

<tbc>_More precisely, there exists a universal constant c\>_0 _such that if_ \(\rho\) _is the resolution of the last phase in which k is sampled, then_

\(\rho\ge c\overline{\Delta_k}.\)

_Proof._ We first consider a suboptimal arm \(k\neq k^\star\).

_Case 1:_ \(\Delta_k\ge 2\varepsilon\) _and_ \(\Delta_k\le\sigma\). Then \(\overline{\Delta_k}=\Delta_k\). Let _j<sub>k</sub>_ be the first phase index such that \(\rho_{j_k}\le\Delta_k\). By dyadicity,<tbc>

\(\frac{\Delta_k}{2}<\rho_{j_k}\le\Delta_k.\)

<tbc>Since \(\Delta_k\ge 2\varepsilon\), we have \(\varepsilon\le\Delta_k/2\). Therefore

\(\varepsilon+\frac{\rho_{j_k}}{4}\le\frac{\Delta_k}{2}+\frac{\Delta_k}{4}=\frac{3\Delta_k}{4}<\Delta_k.\)

Lemma 28 implies that arm _k_ is eliminated by the end of phase _j<sub>k</sub>_, unless the algorithm has already stopped. Thus _k_ is not sampled beyond phase _j<sub>k</sub>_, so its last sampled resolution is at least \(\rho_{j_k}>\overline{\Delta_k}/2\).

_Case 2:_ \(\Delta_k\ge 2\varepsilon\) _and_ \(\Delta_k>\sigma\). Then \(\overline{\Delta_k}=\sigma\). At phase 0, \(\rho_0=\sigma\). Since \(\varepsilon\le\Delta_k/2\) and \(\rho_0/4=\sigma/4<\Delta_k/4\),

\(\varepsilon+\frac{\rho_0}{4}<\frac{\Delta_k}{2}+\frac{\Delta_k}{4}=\frac{3\Delta_k}{4}<\Delta_k.\)

Thus Lemma 28 eliminates arm _k_ by the end of phase 0, unless the algorithm stops. If _k_ is sampled, its last sampled resolution is therefore \(\sigma=\overline{\Delta_k}\).

_Case 3:_ \(\Delta_k<2\varepsilon\). Then \(\overline{\Delta_k}\le 2\varepsilon\). Also \(J=\lceil\mathrm{log}_2(\sigma/\varepsilon)\rceil\), so

\(\rho_J\le\varepsilon<2\rho_J.\)

No arm is sampled after phase _J_. Hence the last sampled resolution satisfies \(\rho\ge\rho_J>\varepsilon/2\ge\overline{\Delta_k}/4\).

Now consider the optimal arm _k<sup>⋆</sup>_, with \(\Delta_{k^\star}=\mathrm{min}_{j\neq k^\star}\Delta_j\). If \(\Delta_{k^\star}\ge 2\varepsilon\) and \(\Delta_{k^\star}\le\sigma\), let _j<sub>⋆</sub>_ be the first phase with \(\rho_{j_\star}\le\Delta_{k^\star}\). The same calculation as in Case 1 shows that every suboptimal arm _a_ satisfies

\(\Delta_a\ge\Delta_{k^\star}>\varepsilon+\frac{\rho_{j_\star}}{4},\)

so all suboptimal arms are eliminated by the end of phase _j<sub>⋆</sub>_, unless the algorithm has already stopped. The active set then becomes singleton and the algorithm returns, so _k<sup>⋆</sup>_ is not sampled beyond this phase and its last sampled resolution exceeds \(\overline{\Delta_{k^\star}}/2\). If \(\Delta_{k^\star}\ge 2\varepsilon\) and \(\Delta_{k^\star}>\sigma\), the same argument applies at phase 0, giving last sampled resolution \(\sigma=\overline{\Delta_{k^\star}}\). If \(\Delta_{k^\star}<2\varepsilon\), the final-phase argument in Case 3 gives last sampled resolution greater than \(\overline{\Delta_{k^\star}}/4\). This proves the claim with _c_=1/4. Early stopping can only increase the last sampled resolution, so no upper bound on it is needed or asserted.

**Lemma 30** (Phased counting bound)**.** _On_ Eph, RESTARTPHASEDCLIP-1BITBAI _uses at most_ \(O\left(\sum_{k=1}^K\Lambda(\overline{\Delta_k})\frac{\sigma^2}{\overline{\Delta_k^2}}\Gamma(\overline{\Delta_k};K,J,\delta)\right)\) _1-bit queries, where_ \(\Lambda(u)=1+log\frac{\sigma}{u}\) _and_ \(\Gamma(u;K,J,\delta)=log\frac{K(J+1)}{\delta}+loglog\left(e^e\frac{\sigma}{u}\right)+loglog\left(e^e\frac{K(J+1)}{\delta}\right).\) _Proof._ By Lemma 27, in phase _j_ each active arm receives at most \(n_j^\circ=O\left(\frac{\alpha_j\sigma^2}{\rho_j^2}\Gamma_j\right)\) queries. Thus the total number of samples of arm _k_ is bounded by \(\sum_{j:\rho_j\unknown\overline{\Delta_k}}O\left(\frac{\alpha_j\sigma^2}{\rho_j^2}\Gamma_j\right).\) Let _jk_ be the last phase in this sum. This index bounds the cost even if the actual last sampled phase is earlier. Hence \(\alpha_{j_k}=1+log\frac{32\sigma}{\rho_{j_k}}=O\big(1+log\frac{\sigma}{\overline{\Delta_k}}\big)=O(\Lambda(\overline{\Delta_k})),\)
\(\frac{\sigma^2}{\rho_{j_k}^2}=O\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{\overline{\Delta_k^2}}\right),\) and \(\Gamma_{j_k}=O\big(\Gamma(\overline{\Delta_k};K,J,\delta)\big).\) Thus arm _k_ contributes at most \(O\left(\Lambda(\overline{\Delta_k})\frac{\sigma^2}{\overline{\Delta_k^2}}\Gamma(\overline{\Delta_k};K,J,\delta)\right).\) Summing this bound over _k_=1_,...,K_ proves the lemma. _Proof of Theorem 10._ By Lemma 24, Eph holds with probability at least \(1-\delta\). <tbc>Therefore

so the reusable phase-_j_ estimator is unbiased for the clipped target _c<sub>k</sub>_+E[[_W<sub>k</sub>]<sub>L<sub>j</sub></sub>_].

We next establish the variance and range bounds needed for Bernstein’s inequality. Conditional on _W<sub>k</sub>=w_,<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}[Z_{k,s}^2|W_k=w]=2A_s\int_{I_s}max\{\sigma,t\}\mathbf{1}\{|w|\ge t\}dt.\)

<tbc>Hence, writing _v<sub>k,s</sub>_:=Var(_Z<sub>k,s</sub>_), we have<tbc>

\(\sum_{s=0}^j\frac{v_{k,s}}{A_s}\le\sum_{s=0}^j\frac{\mathbb{E}[Z_{k,s}^2]}{A_s}\le 2\mathbb{E}\left[\int_0^{L_j}max\{\sigma,t\}\mathbf{1}\{|W_k|\ge t\}dt\right].\)

<tbc>For any \(x\ge 0\),<tbc>

\(\int_0^{L_j}max\{\sigma,t\}\mathbf{1}\{x\ge t\}dt\le\int_0^xmax\{\sigma,t\}dt\le\sigma x+\frac{x^2}{2}.\)

<tbc>Since \(\mathbb{E}[W_k^2]\le 2\sigma^2\), this gives

\(\sum_{s=0}^j\frac{v_{k,s}}{A_s}\le C\sigma^2\)

for a universal constant _C\>_0.

Also,<tbc>

\(|Z_{k,s}|\le\frac{2}{q_s(T)}=2A_smax\{\sigma,T\}\le 2A_sL_s.\)

<tbc>Because \(A_s\ge log2\) for every _s_, the centered variables satisfy

\(|Z_{k,s}-\mathbb{E}Z_{k,s}|\le CA_sL_s\)

for another universal constant _C\>_0.

Now fix a phase _j_. Suppose each slab \(s\le j\) has been topped up to _m<sub>s,j</sub>_ samples. Define

\(\overline{Z_{k,s}}=\frac{1}{m_{s,j}}\sum_{i=1}^{m_{s,j}}Z_{k,s,i}.\)

The centered error of the reusable clipped estimator is

\(\sum_{s=0}^j\left(\overline{Z_{k,s}}-\mathbb{E}Z_{k,s}\right).\)

Its Bernstein variance proxy is<tbc>

\(V_{k,j}:=\sum_{s=0}^j\frac{v_{k,s}}{m_{s,j}},\)

<tbc>and its maximum summand range is<tbc>

\(B_{k,j}:=max_{s\le j}\frac{CA_sL_s}{m_{s,j}}.\)

<tbc>By the choice of _m<sub>s,j</sub>_,<tbc>

\(V_{k,j}\le\frac{\rho_j^2}{C_0\sigma^2\Gamma_j}\sum_{s=0}^j\frac{v_{k,s}}{A_s}\le\frac{C\rho_j^2}{C_0\Gamma_j},\)

<tbc>and

\(B_{k,j}\le max_{s\le j}\frac{CA_sL_s}{C_0A_s\sigma^2\Gamma_j/\rho_j^2}\le\frac{CL_j\rho_j^2}{C_0\sigma^2\Gamma_j}=\frac{32C\rho_j}{C_0\Gamma_j},\)

where the last equality uses \(L_j=32\sigma^2/\rho_j\).

Bernstein’s inequality therefore gives, for a universal constant _c\>_0,

\(Pr\left(\left|\sum_{s=0}^j\left(\overline{Z_{k,s}}-\mathbb{E}Z_{k,s}\right)\right|>2\sqrt{V_{k,j}\Gamma_j}+B_{k,j}\Gamma_j\right)\le e^{-c\Gamma_j}.\)

Since \(\Gamma_j\ge log(K(J+1)/\delta)\), a union bound over all _K(J_+1) arm-phase pairs shows that, with probability at least \(1-\delta\), the above Bernstein bound holds simultaneously for every _k_ and _j_. Taking _C_0 sufficiently large yields \(2\sqrt{V_{k,j}\Gamma_j}+B_{k,j}\Gamma_j\le\frac{3\rho_j}{64}.\) The clipping bias at level _Lj_ is \(\big|\mathbb{E}[W_k]-\mathbb{E}[[W_k]_{L_j}]\big|\le\frac{\sigma^2}{2L_j}=\frac{\rho_j}{64}.\) Consequently, on the simultaneous event, \(\big|\tilde{\mu}_{k,j}^\mathrm{reuse}-\mu_k\big|\le\frac{3\rho_j}{64}+\frac{\rho_j}{64}=\frac{\rho_j}{16}=r_j\) whenever all slabs \(s\le j\) have been topped up to _ms,j_. Thus the reusable estimator certifies the same phase-_j_ radius as the restarted estimator. It remains to count samples. For a fixed arm _k_, let _jk_ be the last phase in which _k_ is sampled by the reusable algorithm. Since samples are retained, the total number of slab samples collected for arm _k_ is bounded by the final top-up target at phase _jk_, namely \(\sum_{s=0}^{j_k}m_{s,j_k}=O\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{\rho_{j_k}^2}\Gamma_{j_k}\sum_{s=0}^{j_k}A_s\right)=O\left(\frac{\alpha_{j_k}\sigma^2}{\rho_{j_k}^2}\Gamma_{j_k}\right).\) On the same valid-interval event, the stopping and elimination arguments from Lemmas 25-29 apply verbatim, since they only use validity of the confidence intervals and the fact that each completed phase reaches radius _rj_. Hence Lemma 29 gives \(\rho_{j_k}\ge c\overline{\Delta_k}.\) Therefore \(\alpha_{j_k}=1+log\frac{32\sigma}{\rho_{j_k}}=O\big(1+log\frac{\sigma}{\overline{\Delta_k}}\big)=O(\Lambda(\overline{\Delta_k})),\)
\(\frac{\sigma^2}{\rho_{j_k}^2}=O\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{\overline{\Delta_k^2}}\right),\) and \(\Gamma_{j_k}=O\big(\Gamma(\overline{\Delta_k};K,J,\delta)\big).\) Thus arm _k_ contributes at most \(O\left(\Lambda(\overline{\Delta_k})\frac{\sigma^2}{\overline{\Delta_k^2}}\Gamma(\overline{\Delta_k};K,J,\delta)\right)\) queries. Summing over _k_=1_,...,K_ proves the claimed bound. ## C.3 Deterministic finite query bounds The high-probability bounds above quantify gap-dependent behavior. _Proof._ In any non-stopping round, if \(k\in\{h,\ell\}\) is sampled, the interval geometry alone gives \(B_h\le 2\beta_k\). Consequently, every sampled arm has \(\beta_\varepsilon(N_k,\delta/K)>\varepsilon/2\). At the deterministic count \(n_\mathrm{fix}^\circ\), its stitched logarithm is exactly the logarithm in the proposition, and

\(2\sqrt{\frac{3\alpha_\varepsilon\sigma^2x_{n_\mathrm{fix}^\circ(\delta/K)}}{n_\mathrm{fix}^\circ}}\le\frac{\varepsilon}{8},\frac{2\alpha_\varepsilon\sigma^2x_{n_\mathrm{fix}^\circ(\delta/K)}}{n_\mathrm{fix}^\circ\varepsilon}\le\frac{\varepsilon}{384}.\)

## C.3.2 Restart phased clipping

**Proposition 33** (Pathwise phased cap)**.** _With_ \(n_j^\circ\) _and_ \(\Gamma_j\) _from Lemma 27, on every realization,_

\(\tau_\mathrm{ph}\le K\sum_{j=0}^Jn_j^\circ=O\big(K\left(1+\mathrm{log}\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}\right)\frac{\sigma^2}{\varepsilon^2}\Gamma_J\big).\)

_Proof._ Lemma 27 gives \(\beta_j(n_j^\circ)\le r_j\) deterministically. An arm reaching \(n_j^\circ\) is therefore never sampled again in that phase. Once all active radii are at most _r<sub>j</sub>_, the algorithm returns or advances to the next phase. ## C.4 Lau-Scarlett estimators with phased successive elimination

We record a batched alternative to make the scope of our rate claim explicit. Use \(\rho_j=2^{-j}\sigma\), \(J=\lceil\mathrm{log}_2(\sigma/\varepsilon)\rceil\), and \(\gamma=\delta/[K(J+1)]\). In phase _j_, invoke the finite-variance fixed-target estimator of Lau and Scarlett \[21\] separately on each active arm with accuracy \(\rho_j/8\) and failure probability \(\gamma\), using the supplied anchor. Retain arms whose estimates are within \(\rho_j/2\) of the largest completed estimate. Return a singleton immediately, or any survivor at phase _J_.

A union bound gives simultaneous accuracy of all completed arm-phase estimates with probability at least \(1-\delta\). On this event, the estimated maximum exceeds the best arm’s estimate by at most \(\rho_j/4\), so the best arm survives. A suboptimal arm with \(\Delta_k>3\rho_j/4\) has estimated deficit greater than \(\rho_j/2\) and is removed. Conversely every survivor has \(\Delta_k\le 3\rho_j/4\), so a final-phase survivor is \(\varepsilon\)-optimal.

The deterministic cost per active arm in phase _j_ is

\(m_j=O\left(\frac{\sigma^2}{\rho_j^2}\left(1+\mathrm{log}\frac{\sigma}{\rho_j}\right)\mathrm{log}\frac{K(J+1)}{\delta}\right).\)

An arm is not sampled at resolutions finer than a constant multiple of \(\overline{\Delta_k}\) on the simultaneous event; for the best arm, all challengers are removed by the corresponding scale. Summing geometrically<tbc>

increasing phase costs gives

\(O\left(\sum_{k=1}^K\frac{\sigma^2}{\Delta_k^2}\left(1+log\frac{\sigma}{\Delta_k}\right)log\frac{K(J+1)}{\delta}\right)=O\left(H_\text{gap}\left[log\frac{K}{\delta}+loglog\left(e^e\frac{\sigma}{\varepsilon}\right)\right]\right).\)

Thus this wrapper matches the leading phased BAI rate. It gives simultaneous confidence at completed checkpoints, while Theorem 5 also provides valid intervals after every intermediate local sample.

## D Proofs for Section 4 (Lower bound) The proof of Theorem 12 establishes an information-theoretic limit by explicitly constructing a "hard pair" of distributions \((\nu_0,\nu_1)\). These distributions are carefully engineered to have a mean gap of exactly \(\Delta\), yet they are geometrically structured so that any single 1-bit measurable set query yields at most \(O(\Delta^2/(J\sigma^2))\) KL information. We then use opposite perturbations to embed this construction into a _K_-arm base instance and alternatives changing one arm at a time, and apply a change-of-measure argument over the predictable \(\sigma\)-algebra of the algorithm’s interaction sequence. ### D.1 Construction of the hard pair Let _J_ be the largest integer such that \(2^{J-1}\le\frac{\sigma}{2\Delta}.\) This definition implies \(\frac{\sigma}{4\Delta}<2^{J-1}\le\frac{\sigma}{2\Delta}\), so taking the base-2 logarithm yields \(J=\lfloor log_2(\frac{\sigma}{\Delta})\rfloor\). Consequently, the number of scales is \(J=\Theta(log\frac{\sigma}{\Delta})\). For each index _i_=1_,...,J_, we define the geometric support scales _mi_ and their corresponding base probability weights _wi_: \(m_i:=2^{i-1},w_i:=\frac{1}{Jm_i^2}.\) To create the mean shift, we introduce the probability mass perturbations \(\xi_i:=\frac{\Delta}{2Jm_i\sigma}.\) To ensure that we can subtract these perturbations without producing negative probabilities, we verify that \(\xi_i\le w_i/4\). By definition, \(\xi_i\le\frac{w_i}{4}\Longleftrightarrow\frac{\Delta}{2Jm_i\sigma}\le\frac{1}{4Jm_i^2}\Longleftrightarrow m_i\le\frac{\sigma}{2\Delta}.\) Since \(m_i=2^{i-1}\le 2^{J-1}\le\frac{\sigma}{2\Delta}\) for all \(i\le J\), the condition holds. We now define the baseline distribution \(\nu_0\) and the perturbed distribution \(\nu_1\) over the finite support \(\{0\}\cup\{\pm m_i\sigma\}_{i=1}^J\): \(\nu_0=\left(1-\sum_{i=1}^Jw_i\right)\delta_0+\sum_{i=1}^J\frac{w_i}{2}\delta_{m_i\sigma}+\sum_{i=1}^J\frac{w_i}{2}\delta_{-m_i\sigma},\)
\(\nu_1=\left(1-\sum_{i=1}^Jw_i\right)\delta_0+\sum_{i=1}^J\left(\frac{w_i}{2}+\xi_i\right)\delta_{m_i\sigma}+\sum_{i=1}^J\left(\frac{w_i}{2}-\xi_i\right)\delta_{-m_i\sigma},\) where \(\delta_x\) denotes the Dirac measure at _x_. Note that the central mass at 0 is strictly positive because \(\sum_{i=1}^Jw_i=\frac{1}{J}\sum_{i=1}^J4^{-(i-1)}<\frac{1}{J}\frac{4}{3}\le 1\) for \(J\ge 2\). **Lemma 34** (Moments of the hard pair)**.** _The distributions_ \(\nu_0\) _and_ \(\nu_1\) _satisfy_ \(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_0}[X]=0,\mathbb{E}_{\nu_1}[X]=\Delta,\) _and have variances bounded by_ \(\sigma^2\). _Proof._ For \(\nu_0\), symmetry across the origin immediately yields \(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_0}[X]=0\). Its second moment expands to exactly the variance proxy: \(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_0}[X^2]=\sum_{i=1}^Jw_i(m_i\sigma)^2=\sum_{i=1}^J\left(\frac{1}{Jm_i^2}\right)m_i^2\sigma^2=\sum_{i=1}^J\frac{\sigma^2}{J}=\sigma^2.\) For \(\nu_1\), the perturbations \(\xi_i\) are explicitly designed to shift the mean. Because the support points are symmetric, the base weights _wi/_2 cancel, leaving only the perturbations: \(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_1}[X]=\sum_{i=1}^J\left[\left(\frac{w_i}{2}+\xi_i\right)(m_i\sigma)+\left(\frac{w_i}{2}-\xi_i\right)(-m_i\sigma)\right]=\sum_{i=1}^J2\xi_im_i\sigma.\)

Substituting \(\xi_i=\frac{\Delta}{2Jm_i\sigma}\), we obtain \(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_1}[X]=\sum_{i=1}^J\frac{\Delta}{J}=\Delta\).

The second moment of \(\nu_1\) remains unchanged because the \(\xi_i\) perturbations are added and subtracted at squared symmetric points:

\(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_1}[X^2]=\sum_{i=1}^J\left[\left(\frac{w_i}{2}+\xi_i\right)(m_i\sigma)^2+\left(\frac{w_i}{2}-\xi_i\right)(-m_i\sigma)^2\right]=\sum_{i=1}^Jw_im_i^2\sigma^2=\sigma^2.\)

Thus, \(\mathrm{Var}_{\nu_1}(X)=\mathbb{E}_{\nu_1}[X^2]-(\mathbb{E}_{\nu_1}[X])^2=\sigma^2-\Delta^2\le\sigma^2\).

For the _K_-arm embedding, write \(P_0:=\nu_0\) and \(P_+:=\nu_1\), and define _P_<sub>-</sub> by reversing the signs of the perturbations:

\(P_-:=\left(1-\sum_{i=1}^Jw_i\right)\delta_0+\sum_{i=1}^J\left(\frac{w_i}{2}-\xi_i\right)\delta_{m_i\sigma}+\sum_{i=1}^J\left(\frac{w_i}{2}+\xi_i\right)\delta_{-m_i\sigma}.\)

By reflection, \(\mathbb{E}_{P_-}[X]=-\Delta\) and \(\mathrm{Var}_{P_-}(X)=\sigma^2-\Delta^2\le\sigma^2\). All three distributions admit the same valid anchor _c_=0, since their means have absolute value at most \(\Delta\le\sigma\).

## D.2 A uniform one-query KL bound

Consider an arbitrary measurable query set \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\). A 1-bit observation \(Y=\mathbf{1}\{X\in A\}\) follows a Bernoulli distribution: Ber(_p_) under \(\nu_0\) and Ber(_q_) under \(\nu_1\), where \(p:=\nu_0(A)\) and \(q:=\nu_1(A)\).

We categorize the scales based on how they intersect with _A_. Let _S(A_) denote the set of index scales \(i\in\{1,\dots,J\}\) where exactly one of the two support points \(\{\pm m_i\sigma\}\) belongs to _A_.

**Lemma 35** (One-query probability difference bound)**.** _For every measurable set_ \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\),<tbc>

\((q-p)^2\le\frac{2\Delta^2}{J\sigma^2}p.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ We analyze the mass difference _q-p_. For any scale \(i\notin S(A)\), either both \(\pm m_i\sigma\in A\) or neither are in _A_. If both are in _A_, the mass difference contributed by scale _i_ is

\((\frac{w_i}{2}+\xi_i)+(\frac{w_i}{2}-\xi_i)-w_i=0.\)

If neither are, the contribution is naturally 0. The origin 0 also contributes equal mass to both distributions.

Thus, only scales in _S(A_) cause a discrepancy. For \(i\in S(A)\), the difference is either \(+\xi_i\) (if \(m_i\sigma\in A\)) or \(-\xi_i\) (if \(-m_i\sigma\in A\)). We can write \(q-p=\sum_{i\in S(A)}s_i\xi_i\) for some signs \(s_i\in\{-1,1\}\). By the triangle inequality:<tbc>

\(|q-p|\le\sum_{i\in S(A)}\xi_i=\frac{\Delta}{2J\sigma}\sum_{i\in S(A)}\frac{1}{m_i}.\)

<tbc>If _S(A_) is empty, then _q-p_=0 and the claimed bound is immediate. Otherwise, let \(S(A)=\{i_1<i_2<\cdots<i_r\}\) be ordered such that _i_<sub>1</sub> is the smallest index. Because _m<sub>i</sub>_ grows geometrically as 2<sup>_i_-1</sup>, the sum is dominated by its largest term:<tbc>

\(\sum_{k=1}^r\frac{1}{m_{i_k}}\le\sum_{k=0}^{r-1}\frac{1}{m_{i_1}2^k}<\frac{2}{m_{i_1}}.\)

<tbc>Squaring this strict bound gives:<tbc>

\(\left(\sum_{i\in S(A)}\frac{1}{m_i}\right)^2<\frac{4}{m_{i_1}^2}.\)

<tbc>Because _i_<sub>1</sub> is an element of _S(A_), we have \(\frac{4}{m_{i_1}^2}\le 4\sum_{i\in S(A)}\frac{1}{m_i^2}\).

Simultaneously, we bound the baseline probability _p_. For every \(i\in S(A)\), exactly one support point is in _A_, contributing _w<sub>i</sub>/_2 to \(\nu_0(A)\). Therefore,<tbc>

\(p\ge\sum_{i\in S(A)}\frac{w_i}{2}=\frac{1}{2J}\sum_{i\in S(A)}\frac{1}{m_i^2}\Longrightarrow\sum_{i\in S(A)}\frac{1}{m_i^2}\le 2Jp.\)

<tbc>Combining these inequalities gives the desired result:

\((q-p)^2\le\frac{\Delta^2}{4J^2\sigma^2}\left(4\sum_{i\in S(A)}\frac{1}{m_i^2}\right)\le\frac{\Delta^2}{J^2\sigma^2}(2Jp)=\frac{2\Delta^2}{J\sigma^2}p.\)

**Lemma 36** (Uniform KL divergence bound)**.** _There exists an absolute constant C_<sub>0</sub>_\>_0 _such that for every measurable set_ \(A\subseteq\mathbb{R}\),<tbc>

\(max\{kl(q,p),kl(p,q)\}\le C_0\frac{\Delta^2}{J\sigma^2},\)

<tbc>_where_ \(kl(u,v)=ulog\frac{u}{v}+(1-u)log\frac{1-u}{1-v}\) _denotes the binary KL divergence. Moreover, writing_ \(p_\pm:=P_\pm(A)\)_, the opposite perturbations satisfy_<tbc>

\(max\{kl(p_-,p_+),kl(p_+,p_-)\}\le 4C_0\frac{\Delta^2}{J\sigma^2}.\)

<tbc>_Proof._ If _p_=0 or _p_=1, the perturbed laws assign the same probability to _A_, so all divergences vanish. Otherwise, we first establish that the likelihood ratio is bounded, specifically that<tbc>

\(\frac{q}{p}\in\left[\frac{1}{2},\frac{3}{2}\right].\)

<tbc>Using the structural properties of our construction, we bounded \(\xi_i\le w_i/4\). Therefore:<tbc>

\(|q-p|\le\sum_{i\in S(A)}\xi_i\le\frac{1}{4}\sum_{i\in S(A)}w_i=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{i\in S(A)}\frac{w_i}{2}\le\frac{1}{2}p.\)

<tbc>This implies \(-\frac{1}{2}p\le q-p\le\frac{1}{2}p\), which rearranges exactly to \(\frac{1}{2}p\le q\le\frac{3}{2}p\).

By complement invariance of binary KL divergence, kl(_q,p_)=kl(1-_q,_1-_p_). We may assume without loss of generality that \(p\le 1/2\) (if not, we simply replace _A_ with its complement _A<sup>c</sup>_, noting that _S(A_)=_S(A<sup>c</sup>_)).

Using the standard inequality \(kl(u,v)\le\frac{(u-v)^2}{v(1-v)}\) and Lemma 35, we obtain:<tbc>

\(kl(q,p)\le\frac{(q-p)^2}{p(1-p)}\le\frac{(q-p)^2}{p(1/2)}=2\frac{(q-p)^2}{p}\le 4\frac{\Delta^2}{J\sigma^2}.\)

<tbc>To bound the reverse direction kl(_p,q_), we require _q_(1-_q_) in the denominator. Since \(p\le 1/2\), our likelihood bounds give \(q\le 3/4\), meaning \(1-q\ge 1/4\). Furthermore, \(q\ge p/2\). Therefore, \(q(1-q)\ge(p/2)(1/4)=p/8\). Thus:<tbc>

\(kl(p,q)\le\frac{(p-q)^2}{q(1-q)}\le 8\frac{(q-p)^2}{p}\le 16\frac{\Delta^2}{J\sigma^2}.\)

<tbc>The first bound holds with the absolute constant _C_<sub>0</sub>=16. For the opposite perturbations, _p_<sub>+</sub>=_q_ and _p_<sub>-</sub>=2_p-q_, so \(|p_\pm-p|\le p/2\). With \(p\le 1/2\) as above, both denominators satisfy \(p_\pm(1-p_\pm)\ge p/8\). Since _p_<sub>+</sub>-_p_<sub>-</sub>=2(_q-p_), the same binary KL inequality gives

\(max\{kl(p_-,p_+),kl(p_+,p_-)\}\le 8\frac{4(q-p)^2}{p}\le 64\frac{\Delta^2}{J\sigma^2}=4C_0\frac{\Delta^2}{J\sigma^2}.\)

The law of _U_ is the same under every instance. Consequently, both the stopping time \(\tau\) and the final arm recommendation \(\widehat{k}\) are measurable with respect to the infinite-horizon \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal{F}_\infty=\sigma\big(\bigcup_{t=1}^\infty\mathcal{F}_t\big)\).

**Lemma 37** (Data processing for the error event)**.** _If the algorithm is_ \(\delta\)_-correct over the instance class, then for each_ \(i\ge 2\)

\(\mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{Pr}_0,\mathrm{Pr}_i)\ge c_1\mathrm{log}(1/\delta)\)

_for an absolute constant c_<sub>1</sub>_\>_0_. The same conclusion holds for_ \((\varepsilon,\delta)\)_-PAC algorithms when_ \(0<\varepsilon<\Delta/2\)_, since only the unique best arm is_ \(\varepsilon\)_-optimal in either instance._

_Proof._ Let \(E:=\{\widehat{k}=1\}\) be the event that the algorithm recommends arm 1. By the \(\delta\)-correctness requirement, the algorithm must identify the correct arm with probability at least \(1-\delta\). Therefore, \(\mathrm{Pr}_0(E)\ge 1-\delta\) and \(\mathrm{Pr}_i(E)\le\delta\). Because the recommendation \(\widehat{k}\) is entirely determined by the full transcript \((U,(Z_t)_{t\ge 1})\), the data-processing inequality implies:<tbc>

\(\mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{Pr}_0,\mathrm{Pr}_i)\ge\mathrm{kl}(\mathrm{Pr}_0(E),\mathrm{Pr}_i(E))\ge\mathrm{kl}(1-\delta,\delta).\)

<tbc>For any \(\delta\in(0,1/4)\),

\(\mathrm{kl}(1-\delta,\delta)\ge(1-2\delta)\mathrm{log}\frac{1-\delta}{\delta}\ge c_1\mathrm{log}(1/\delta)\)

for some _c_<sub>1</sub>_\>_0.

**Lemma 38** (Transcript divergence bound)**.** _For each_ \(i\ge 2\), \(\mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{Pr}_0,\mathrm{Pr}_i)\le 4C_0\frac{\Delta^2}{J\sigma^2}\mathbb{E}_0[N_i(\tau)]\).

_Proof._ Fix \(i\ge 2\). Let \(\mathrm{Pr}_0^{(T)}\) and \(\mathrm{Pr}_i^{(T)}\) denote the marginal laws of the truncated transcript (_U,Z_<sub>1:_T_</sub>). By the chain rule for relative entropy:

\(\mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{Pr}_0^{(T)},\mathrm{Pr}_i^{(T)})=\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb{E}_0\big[\mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{Pr}_0^{(T)}|U,Z_{1:t-1})\|\mathrm{Pr}_i(Z_t|U,Z_{1:t-1}))\big].\)

Let F<sub>_t_-1</sub> be the \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by (_U,Z_<sub>1:_t_-1</sub>). Conditioned on F<sub>_t_-1</sub>, the event \(\{t\le\tau\}\) is determined.

If \(t>\tau\), the process has stopped, and \(Z_t=(1,\emptyset,\perp)\) is deterministic under both instances. The conditional KL divergence is exactly 0.

If \(t\le\tau\), the arm _K<sub>t</sub>_ and query set _A<sub>t</sub>_ are deterministic functions of F<sub>_t_-1</sub>. The only randomness lies in the Bernoulli observation _Y<sub>t</sub>_. If \(K_t\neq i\), its distribution is unchanged between \(\nu^{(0)}\) and \(\nu^{(i)}\), so the conditional divergence is 0. If _K<sub>t</sub>=i_, then _Y<sub>t</sub>_∼Ber(_P_<sub>-</sub>(_A<sub>t</sub>_)) under \(\nu^{(0)}\) and _Y<sub>t</sub>_∼Ber(_P_<sub>+</sub>(_A<sub>t</sub>_)) under \(\nu^{(i)}\). By Lemma 36, the conditional divergence is bounded by \(4C_0\Delta^2/(J\sigma^2)\). Thus:

\(\mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{Pr}_0^{(T)},\mathrm{Pr}_i^{(T)})\le\sum_{t=1}^T\mathbb{E}_0\left[\mathbf{1}\{t\le\tau,K_t=i\}4C_0\frac{\Delta^2}{J\sigma^2}\right]=4C_0\frac{\Delta^2}{J\sigma^2}\mathbb{E}_0[N_i(T\wedge\tau)].\)

Because F_<sub>T</sub>_ forms an increasing filtration generating the full transcript, \(\mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{Pr}_0,\mathrm{Pr}_i)=\mathrm{lim}_{T\rightarrow\infty}\mathrm{KL}(\mathrm{Pr}_0^{(T)},\mathrm{Pr}_i^{(T)})\). Applying the monotone convergence theorem to \(N_i(T\wedge\tau)\) yields the final bound.

_Proof of Theorem 12._ Assuming \(\mathbb{E}_0[\tau]<\infty\) (otherwise the lower bound holds trivially), we link the information complexity from Lemma 38 to the statistical requirement from Lemma 37, for each _i_=2_,...,K_:<tbc>

\(4C_0\frac{\Delta^2}{J\sigma^2}\mathbb{E}_0[N_i(\tau)]\ge c_1\mathrm{log}\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right).\)

<tbc>Rearranging this inequality for the expected sample complexity yields:<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}_0[N_i(\tau)]\ge\frac{c_1}{4C_0}\frac{\sigma^2J}{\Delta^2}\mathrm{log}\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right).\)

<tbc>All these inequalities hold under the same base instance. Summing over its _K_-1 suboptimal arms gives<tbc>

\(\mathbb{E}_0[\tau]\ge\sum_{i=2}^K\mathbb{E}_0[N_i(\tau)]\ge\frac{c_1}{4C_0}(K-1)\frac{\sigma^2J}{\Delta^2}\mathrm{log}\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right).\)

<tbc>Recalling our construction choice that \(J=\lfloor\mathrm{log}_2(\frac{\sigma}{\Delta})\rfloor\), it holds that \(J\ge c_2\mathrm{log}(\frac{\sigma}{\Delta})\) for some constant _c_<sub>2</sub>_\>_0 given the restriction \(\Delta\le\sigma/4\). Substituting this structural scale count gives:

\(\mathbb{E}_0[\tau]\ge c(K-1)\frac{\sigma^2}{\Delta^2}\mathrm{log}\left(\frac{\sigma}{\Delta}\right)\mathrm{log}\left(\frac{1}{\delta}\right),\)

where \(c=\frac{c_1c_2}{4C_0}>0\) is an absolute constant, completing the proof.

### Algorithms and Exploration Parameter Tuning

We evaluate three variations of our 1-bit algorithm--FIXEDCLIP, RESTARTPHASE, and REUSEPHASE--against the full-feedback UGAPE baseline.

In practice, theoretically derived confidence intervals can be overly conservative. For the empirical comparison, we introduce a constant exploration multiplier to the leading confidence radius term. For the 1-bit algorithms, this is implemented as an `exploration` parameter that directly scales the logarithmic \(x_n(\gamma)\) term within the tail-integral confidence bounds.

The exploration parameters were tuned as follows:

• **FIXEDCLIP**: The exploration parameter was tuned to 0.04 for the Bernoulli environment and 0.05 for the Normal and Student-t environments.<tbc>

• **RESTARTPHASE & REUSEPHASE**: The exploration parameter was consistently set to 0.03 across all three environments.<tbc>

• **UGAPE Baseline**: The exploration constant _c_ scaling the empirical Bernstein/Hoeffding radius was tuned per environment to 0.06 for Bernoulli, 0.0002 for Normal, and 0.0005 for Student-t.

### UGAPE Modifications for Unbounded Support

For bounded-support environments (e.g., Bernoulli), the UGAPE baseline uses the raw full-feedback rewards. However, for unbounded- support environments (such as the Normal and Student-t settings), the UGAPE baseline is modified to include finite-variance clipping. In these unbounded settings, it still receives full continuous feedback, but it clips every observed reward around the arm’s anchor using the same fixed clipping scale _L_ as the FIXEDCLIP algorithm. The corresponding finite-variance clipping bias is then explicitly added to the algorithm’s confidence radius.

The reported empirical error frequencies remain at or below the target \(\delta\) in the tested configurations. Reducing the exploration multipliers below their theorem values and imposing the experimental query cap do not preserve the proved PAC guarantee automatically. These results are empirical assessments of the tuned implementations; Theorems 8 and 10 concern the stated, untuned confidence radii and stopping rules.

All numerical simulations were executed on a dedicated Linux workstation equipped with an Intel(R) Core(TM) Ultra 9 285K processor (24 cores, up to 5.1 GHz) and 128 GB of RAM.
